title: Lviv Rushhour: Bidirectional Dijkstra Cuts Search!
description: Watch how Bidirectional Dijkstra shrinks the route-finding space by expanding shortest-path frontiers from both start and goal. On real street-map graphs, it meets in the middle to find optimal paths faster than single-direction search.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Lviv (Stare Misto) turns into a living weighted graph! 

🔍 In this visualization, **Bidirectional Dijkstra** runs two synchronized searches: one forward from the start and one backward from the destination. Each side maintains a priority queue of nodes by current best distance (classic Dijkstra’s relaxation), but instead of expanding the entire graph, they progress until their explored regions intersect. When the frontiers meet, we can combine the partial shortest distances to produce the **globally optimal** route over **nonnegative edge weights** (roads with costs like travel time or distance). 

📌 From a graph theory perspective, we’re essentially finding the shortest path in a weighted directed/undirected street graph by using a meet-in-the-middle strategy—dramatically reducing the number of expanded vertices on typical road networks. 

💡 Want to see how different cost functions (time vs distance) change the chosen path? Drop a 🧠 in the comments and tell me your favorite weighting idea! 

▶️ Like, save, and follow for more real-map algorithm reels!
fb_caption:
🧠🚦 Lviv’s streets become a weighted graph for a shortest-path showdown! 

In this run, **Bidirectional Dijkstra** explores from both the start and the destination at the same time. By relaxing edges with priority queues in two directions and stopping when the searches meet, it finds the optimal path while expanding far fewer nodes than one-way search. 

📣 Have questions about how frontier meeting works or how weights affect routes? Comment below—and share this post with a friend who loves coding + graph algorithms!

✅ You’ll learn: weighted graph shortest path, priority-queue expansions, edge relaxation, and why bidirectional search can reduce explored nodes on real road networks.
